'''Eugenio Calabi''' (May 11, 1923 – September 25, 2023) was an Italian-born American mathematician and the [[Thomas A. Scott Professorship of Mathematics|Thomas A. Scott Professor of Mathematics]] at the [[University of Pennsylvania]], specializing in [[differential geometry]], [[partial differential equation]]s and their applications.

==Early life and education==
Calabi was born in [[Milan|Milan, Italy]] on May 11, 1923, into a [[Italian Jews|Jewish]] family.<ref>American Men and Women of Science, Thomson Gale 2004</ref> His sister was the journalist [[Tullia Zevi|Tullia Zevi Calabi]]. In 1938, the family left Italy because of the [[Italian racial laws|racial laws]],  and in 1939 arrived in the United States.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Calabi |first1=Eugenio |title=A Tribute to the Italian-Jewish Journalist Tullia Calabi Zevi |url=https://italian.sas.upenn.edu/events/2012/01/24/tribute-italian-jewish-journalist-tullia-calabi-zevi |publisher=[[University of Pennsylvania School of Arts and Sciences|Penn Arts & Sciences]], Italian Studies |date=January 24, 2012}}</ref><ref name="linda">{{cite web |last1=Arntzenius |first1=Linda |title=Oral History Project: Eugenio Calabi Interviewed by Linda Arntzenius |url=https://albert.ias.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/4078e85f-10c3-4eed-8df7-dbb9a0f60479/content |publisher=Shelby White and Leon Levy Archives Center, Institute for Advanced Study |date=January 21, 2016}}</ref>

In the fall of 1939, aged only 16, Calabi enrolled at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], studying [[chemical engineering]]. His studies were interrupted when he was [[Conscription in the United States|drafted in the US military]] in 1943 and served during [[World War II]]. Upon his discharge in 1946, Calabi was able to finish his bachelor's degree under the [[G.I. Bill]], and was a [[William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition|Putnam Fellow]].<ref name="linda" /><ref name="MMA">{{cite web |title=Putnam Competition Individual and Team Winners |url=http://www.maa.org/programs/maa-awards/putnam-competition-individual-and-team-winners |access-date=December 10, 2021 |publisher=[[Mathematical Association of America]]}}</ref> He received a master's degree in mathematics from the [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign]] in 1947 and his [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in mathematics from [[Princeton University]] in 1950. His doctoral dissertation, titled "Isometric complex analytic imbedding of [[Kähler manifold]]s", was done under the supervision of [[Salomon Bochner]].<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=8111}}</ref>

==Academic career==
From 1951 to 1955 he was an assistant professor at [[Louisiana State University]], and he moved to the [[University of Minnesota]] in 1955, where he became a full professor in 1960. In 1964, Calabi joined the mathematics faculty at the [[University of Pennsylvania]]. Following the retirement of [[Hans Rademacher]], he was appointed to the [[Thomas A. Scott Professorship of Mathematics]] at the University of Pennsylvania in 1968. In 1994, Calabi assumed [[emeritus]] status, and in 2014 the university awarded him an [[Honorary degree|honorary doctorate of science]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://almanac.upenn.edu/archive/volumes/v60/n23/commencementspeaker2014.html|title=Penn's 2014 Commencement Speaker and Honorary Degree Recipients|volume=60|issue=23|date=February 18, 2014|work=University of Pennsylvania Almanac}}</ref><ref name="inquirer">{{cite news|last=Miles|first=Gary|url=https://www.inquirer.com/obituaries/eugenio-calabi-obituary-pennsylvania-philadelphia-mathematician-italy-20230928.html|title=Eugenio Calabi, child prodigy, renowned mathematician, and professor emeritus at Penn, has died at 100|date=September 28, 2023 |access-date=September 29, 2023|work=[[The Philadelphia Inquirer]]}}</ref><ref name="notices">{{cite journal|journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]]|date=October 1991|volume=38|issue=8|title=1991 Steele Prizes Awarded in Orono|url=https://www.ams.org/journals/notices/199110/199110FullIssue.pdf?cat=fullissue&trk=fullissue199110}}</ref>

In 1982, Calabi was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/eugenio-calabi-gesa4a/|access-date=October 1, 2023|website=[[National Academy of Sciences]]|title=Eugenio Calabi}}</ref> He won the [[Leroy P. Steele Prize]] from the [[American Mathematical Society]] in 1991, where his "fundamental work on global differential geometry, especially complex differential geometry" was cited as having "profoundly changed the landscape of the field".<ref name="notices" /> In 2012, he became a fellow of the American Mathematical Society.<ref>[https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society], retrieved November 10, 2012.</ref> In 2021, he was awarded Commander of the [[Order of Merit of the Italian Republic]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Official Gazette of the Italian Republic, 2022 March 17|url=https://www.gazzettaufficiale.it/do/gazzetta/downloadPdf?dataPubblicazioneGazzetta=20220317&numeroGazzetta=64&tipoSerie=SG&tipoSupplemento=SO&numeroSupplemento=11&progressivo=0&estensione=pdf&edizione=0}}</ref><ref name="inquirer" />

Calabi married Giuliana Segre in 1952, with whom he had a son and a daughter. He died on September 25, 2023, aged 100.<ref name="inquirer" /><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ihes.fr/en/tribute-to-eugenio-calabi|title=Tribute to Eugenio Calabi|date=September 27, 2023|publisher=[[Institut des Hautes Études Scientifiques]]}}</ref>

==Research==
Calabi made a number of contributions to the field of [[differential geometry]]. Other contributions, not discussed here, include the construction of a holomorphic version of the [[long line (topology)|long line]] with [[Maxwell Rosenlicht]], a study of the [[moduli space]] of [[space form]]s, a characterization of when a [[Riemannian metric|metric]] can be found so that a given [[differential form]] is harmonic, and various works on [[affine geometry]]. In the comments on his collected works in 2021, Calabi cited his article "Improper affine hyperspheres of convex type and a generalization of a theorem by K. Jörgens" as that which he was "most proud of".{{sfnm|1a1=Calabi|1y=2021}}

===Kähler geometry===
At the 1954 [[International Congress of Mathematicians]], Calabi announced a theorem on how the [[Ricci curvature]] of a [[Kähler manifold|Kähler metric]] could be prescribed.{{ran|C54}} He later found that his proof, via the [[method of continuity]], was flawed, and the result became known as the [[Calabi conjecture]]. In 1957, Calabi published a paper in which the conjecture was stated as a proposition, but with an openly incomplete proof.{{ran|C57}} He gave a complete proof that any solution of the problem must be uniquely defined, but was only able to reduce the problem of existence to the problem of establishing ''[[a priori estimate]]s'' for certain [[partial differential equation]]s. In the 1970s, [[Shing-Tung Yau]] began working on the Calabi conjecture, initially attempting to disprove it. After several years of work, he found a proof of the conjecture, and was able to establish several striking [[algebraic geometry|algebro-geometric]] consequences of its validity. As a particular case of the conjecture, Kähler metrics with zero Ricci curvature are established on a number of [[complex manifold]]s; these are now known as ''Calabi–Yau metrics''. They have become significant in [[string theory]] research since the 1980s.<ref name="besse">{{cite book|last1=Besse|first1=Arthur L.|title=Einstein manifolds|series=Ergebnisse der Mathematik und ihrer Grenzgebiete (3)|volume=10|publisher=[[Springer-Verlag]]|location=Berlin|year=1987|isbn=3-540-15279-2|mr=0867684|others=Reprinted in 2008|doi=10.1007/978-3-540-74311-8|author-link1=Arthur Besse|zbl=0613.53001}}</ref><ref name="beckerbeckerschwarz">{{cite book|mr=2285203|last1=Becker|first1=Katrin|last2=Becker|author-link3=John Henry Schwarz|first2=Melanie|last3=Schwarz|first3=John H.|title=String theory and M-theory. A modern introduction|zbl=1123.81001|doi=10.1017/CBO9780511816086|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|location=Cambridge|year=2007|isbn=978-0-521-86069-7}}</ref><ref name="yaubook">{{cite book|last1=Yau|first1=Shing-Tung|last2=Nadis|first2=Steve|zbl=1435.32001|title=The shape of a life. One mathematician's search for the universe's hidden geometry|publisher=[[Yale University Press]]|location=New Haven, CT|year=2019|isbn=978-0-300-23590-6|mr=3930611|author-link1=Shing-Tung Yau}}</ref>

In 1982, Calabi introduced a [[geometric flow]], now known as the [[Calabi flow]], as a proposal for finding Kähler metrics of constant [[scalar curvature]].{{ran|C82a}} More broadly, Calabi introduced the notion of an [[extremal Kähler metric]], and established (among other results) that they provide strict global minima of the ''Calabi functional'' and that any constant scalar curvature metric is also a global minimum.{{ran|C85}} Later, Calabi and [[Xiuxiong Chen]] made an extensive study of the metric introduced by [[Toshiki Mabuchi]], and showed that the Calabi flow contracts the Mabuchi distance between any two Kähler metrics.{{ran|CC02}} Furthermore, they showed that the Mabuchi metric endows the space of Kähler metrics with the structure of a [[Alexandrov space]] of nonpositive curvature. The technical difficulty of their work is that geodesics in their infinite-dimensional context may have low differentiability.<ref name="besse" />

A well-known construction of Calabi's puts complete Kähler metrics on the total spaces of hermitian vector bundles whose curvature is bounded below.{{ran|C79}} In the case that the base is a complete Kähler–Einstein manifold and the vector bundle has rank one and constant curvature, one obtains a complete Kähler–Einstein metric on the total space. In the case of the cotangent bundle of a complex space form, one obtains a [[Hyperkähler manifold|hyperkähler metric]]. The [[Eguchi–Hanson space]] is a special case of Calabi's construction.<ref name="besse" />

===Geometric analysis===
Calabi found the ''Laplacian comparison theorem'' in [[Riemannian geometry]], which relates the [[Laplace–Beltrami operator]], as applied to the [[Riemannian metric|Riemannian distance function]], to the Ricci curvature.{{ran|C58a}} The Riemannian distance function is generally not differentiable everywhere, which poses a difficulty in formulating a global version of the theorem. Calabi made use of a generalized notion of differential inequalities, predating the later [[viscosity solution]]s introduced by [[Michael G. Crandall|Michael Crandall]] and [[Pierre-Louis Lions]]. By extending the [[strong maximum principle]] of [[Eberhard Hopf]] to his notion of viscosity solutions, Calabi was able to use his Laplacian comparison theorem to extend recent results of [[Joseph Keller]] and [[Robert Osserman]] to Riemannian contexts. Further extensions, based on different uses of the [[maximum principle]], were later found by [[Shiu-Yuen Cheng]] and Yau, among others.<ref name="besse" /><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Cheng|first1=S. Y.|author-link1=Shiu-Yuen Cheng|last2=Yau|first2=S. T.|zbl=0312.53031|title=Differential equations on Riemannian manifolds and their geometric applications|journal=[[Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics]]|volume=28|year=1975|issue=3|pages=333–354|mr=0385749|doi=10.1002/cpa.3160280303|author-link2=Shing-Tung Yau}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Petersen|first1=Peter|title=Riemannian geometry|edition=Third edition of 1998 original|series=[[Graduate Texts in Mathematics]]|volume=171|publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]]|location= Cham|year=2016|isbn=978-3-319-26652-7|mr=3469435|doi=10.1007/978-3-319-26654-1|zbl=1417.53001}}</ref>

{{anchor|Bernstein problem}}In parallel to the classical [[Bernstein problem]] for [[minimal surface]]s, Calabi considered the analogous problem for [[maximal surface]]s, settling the question in low dimensions.{{ran|C70}} An unconditional answer for the '''Bernstein problem for maximal surfaces''' was found later by [[Shiu-Yuen Cheng]] and [[Shing-Tung Yau]], making use of the ''Calabi trick'' that Calabi had pioneered to circumvent the non-differentiability of the Riemannian distance function. In analogous work, Calabi had earlier considered the convex solutions of the [[Monge–Ampère equation]] which are defined on all of [[Euclidean space]] and with 'right-hand side' equal to one. [[Konrad Jörgens]] had earlier studied this problem for functions of two variables, proving that any solution is a quadratic polynomial. By interpreting the problem as one of [[affine geometry]], Calabi was able to apply his earlier work on the Laplacian comparison theorem to extend Jörgens' work to some higher dimensions.{{ran|C58b}} The problem was completely resolved later by [[Aleksei Pogorelov]], and the result is commonly known as the ''Jörgens–Calabi–Pogorelov theorem''.<ref name="nomizu">{{cite book|first1=Katsumi|last1=Nomizu|first2=Takeshi|author-link=Katsumi Nomizu|last2=Sasaki|title=Affine differential geometry|year=1994|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|location=|isbn=0-521-44177-3|mr=1311248|zbl=0834.53002}}</ref>

Later, Calabi considered the problem of [[affine sphere|affine hyperspheres]], first characterizing such surfaces as those for which the [[Legendre transform]] solves a certain Monge–Ampère equation. By adapting his earlier methods in extending Jörgens' theorem, Calabi was able to classify the complete affine elliptic hyperspheres.{{ran|C72}} Further results were later obtained by Cheng and Yau.<ref name="nomizu" /><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Cheng|first1=Shiu Yuen|author-link1=Shiu-Yuen Cheng|last2=Yau|first2=Shing-Tung|zbl=0623.53002|title=Complete affine hypersurfaces. I. The completeness of affine metrics|journal=[[Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics]]|volume=39|year=1986|issue=6|pages=839–866|mr=0859275|doi=10.1002/cpa.3160390606|author-link2=Shing-Tung Yau}}</ref>

===Differential geometry===
Calabi and [[Beno Eckmann]] discovered the [[Calabi–Eckmann manifold]] in 1953.{{ran|CE53}} It is notable as a [[simply-connected]] complex manifold which does not admit any [[Kähler manifold|Kähler metrics]].<ref>{{cite book|mr=0533884|title=Complex manifolds without potential theory|last1=Chern|first1=Shiing Shen|series=Universitext|publisher=[[Springer-Verlag]]|location=New York–Heidelberg|year=1979|isbn=0-387-90422-0|doi=10.1007/978-1-4684-9344-3|zbl=0444.32004|author-link1=Shiing-Shen Chern}}</ref><ref name="blair">{{cite book|last1=Blair|first1=David E.|title=Riemannian geometry of contact and symplectic manifolds|edition=Second edition of 2002 original|series=Progress in Mathematics|volume=203|publisher=[[Birkhäuser]]|location=Boston, MA|year=2010|mr=2682326|isbn=978-0-8176-4958-6|doi=10.1007/978-0-8176-4959-3|zbl=1246.53001}}</ref>

Inspired by recent work of [[Kunihiko Kodaira]], Calabi and [[Edoardo Vesentini]] considered the infinitesimal rigidity of compact holomorphic quotients of [[Cartan domain]]s.{{ran|CV60}} Making use of the [[Bochner's formula|Bochner technique]] and Kodaira's developments of [[sheaf cohomology]], they proved the rigidity of higher-dimensional cases. Their work was an influence on the later work of [[George Mostow]] and [[Grigori Margulis]], who established their global rigidity results out of attempts to understand infinitesimal rigidity results such as Calabi and Vesentini's, along with related works by [[Atle Selberg]] and [[André Weil]].<ref>{{cite book|author-link1=Jürgen Jost|last1=Jost|title=Riemannian geometry and geometric analysis|first1=Jürgen|edition=Seventh edition of 1995 original|series=Universitext|publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]]|location= Cham|year=2017|isbn=978-3-319-61859-3|mr=3726907|doi=10.1007/978-3-319-61860-9|zbl=1380.53001}}</ref>

Calabi and Lawrence Markus considered the problem of [[space form]]s of positive curvature in [[Lorentzian manifold|Lorentzian geometry]].{{ran|CM62}} Their results, which [[Joseph A. Wolf]] considered "very surprising",{{sfnm|1a1=Calabi|1a2=Markus|1y=1962|1loc=MR review}} assert that the [[fundamental group]] must be finite, and that the corresponding group of isometries of [[de Sitter space]]time (under an orientability condition) will act faithfully by isometries on an equatorial sphere. As such, their space form problem reduces to the problem of [[space form|Riemannian space forms]] of positive curvature.<ref>{{cite book|author-link1=Stephen Hawking|author-link2=George F. R. Ellis|last1=Hawking|last2=Ellis|title-link=The Large Scale Structure of Space–Time|title=The large scale structure of space-time|first1=S. W.|first2=G. F. R.|series=Cambridge Monographs on Mathematical Physics|volume=1|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|location=London−New York|year=1973|isbn=0-521-20016-4|doi=10.1017/CBO9780511524646|mr=0424186|zbl=0265.53054}}</ref><ref>{{cite book | last = Wolf | first = Joseph A. | edition = Sixth edition of 1967 original | isbn = 978-0-8218-5282-8 | mr = 2742530 | publisher = [[Chelsea Publishing Company|AMS Chelsea Publishing]]|location=Providence, RI | title = Spaces of constant curvature  | year = 2011|author-link1=Joseph A. Wolf|zbl=1216.53003|doi=10.1090/chel/372}}.</ref>

Work of [[John Forbes Nash Jr.|John Nash]] in the 1950s considered the problem of [[isometric embedding]]s. His work showed that such embeddings are very flexible and deformable. In his PhD thesis, Calabi had previously considered the special case of holomorphic isometric embeddings into [[space form|complex-geometric space forms]].{{ran|C53}} A striking result of his shows that such embeddings are completely determined by the intrinsic geometry and the curvature of the space form in question. Moreover, he was able to study the problem of existence via his introduction of the ''diastatic function'', which is a locally defined function built from [[Kähler manifold|Kähler potentials]] and which mimics the Riemannian distance function. Calabi proved that a holomorphic isometric embedding must preserve the diastatic function. As a consequence, he was able to obtain a criterion for local existence of holomorphic isometric embeddings.<ref name="blair" />

Later, Calabi studied the two-dimensional [[minimal surface]]s (of high codimension) in round spheres.{{ran|C67}} He proved that the area of topologically spherical minimal surfaces can only take on a discrete set of values, and that the surfaces themselves are classified by [[rational curve]]s in a certain [[hermitian symmetric space]].<ref>{{cite book|mr=2044031|title=Harmonic morphisms between Riemannian manifolds|last1=Baird|first1=Paul|last2=Wood|first2=John C.|author-link2=John C. Wood|series=London Mathematical Society Monographs (New Series)|volume=29|publisher=[[Oxford University Press|The Clarendon Press, Oxford University Press]]|location=Oxford|year=2003|isbn=0-19-850362-8|zbl=1055.53049|doi=10.1093/acprof:oso/9780198503620.001.0001}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|mr=0679067|title=Conformal and minimal immersions of compact surfaces into the 4-sphere|last1=Bryant|first1=Robert L.|author-link1=Robert Bryant (mathematician)|journal=[[Journal of Differential Geometry]]|volume=17|year=1982|issue=3|pages=455–473|doi=10.4310/jdg/1214437137|doi-access=free|zbl=0498.53046}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|mr=0703510|title=Selected topics in harmonic maps|last1=Eells|first1=James|author-link1=James Eells|last2=Lemaire|first2=Luc|series=CBMS Regional Conference Series in Mathematics|volume=50|publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]]|location=Providence, RI|year=1983|isbn=0-8218-0700-5|doi=10.1090/cbms/050|zbl=0515.58011}}</ref>

Calabi was the author of fewer than fifty research articles.
